prompt: Which general pattern is a reliable sign that a structure has two resonance forms?

choices.text: A three-atom grouping with a p orbital on each atom
Any atom bearing a negative charge
choices.why: A charge alone isn't enough; the charged atom's p orbital must sit next to a multiple bond in a three-atom grouping.

choices.text: Any two atoms joined by a single bond
choices.why: Resonance needs π or nonbonding electrons that can shift; a lone σ bond has none.

choices.text: Any ring of six carbon atoms
choices.why: Rings aren't the requirement. The pattern is a three-atom grouping with a p orbital on each atom.

explanation: In general, any three-atom grouping with a p orbital on each atom has two resonance forms. Recognizing such groupings within larger structures lets you generate resonance forms systematically.

prompt: How many resonance forms does a single three-atom grouping X=Y–Z*, with a p orbital on each atom, have?
explanation: Any three-atom grouping with a p orbital on each atom has two resonance forms. They differ by exchanging the multiple bond and the asterisk from one end of the grouping to the other.

prompt: In the general three-atom grouping X=Y–Z*, what can the asterisk on atom Z stand for?

choices.text: A p orbital that is vacant, holds a single electron, or holds a lone pair
Only a lone pair of electrons
choices.why: A lone pair is one possibility, but the p orbital can also be vacant (as in a cation) or hold one electron (as in a radical).

choices.text: Only a negative charge
choices.why: The asterisk describes the p orbital's contents, which can be empty, one electron, or a lone pair.

choices.text: A hydrogen atom that moves between the end atoms
choices.why: Atoms never move between resonance forms; the asterisk marks a p orbital.

explanation: The asterisk might mean that the p orbital on atom Z is vacant, that it contains a single electron, or that it contains a lone pair of electrons.

prompt: How do the two resonance forms of a three-atom grouping X=Y–Z* differ?

choices.text: The multiple bond and the asterisk exchange positions, from one end of the grouping to the other
Atoms X and Z trade places
choices.why: Atoms stay where they are; only the multiple bond and the p-orbital contents swap ends.

choices.text: The middle atom Y gains the asterisk
choices.why: The asterisk moves from Z to X, the other end of the grouping, not to Y.

choices.text: The double bond becomes a triple bond
choices.why: The bond order doesn't increase; the multiple bond simply moves to the other side of Y.

explanation: The two resonance forms differ simply by an exchange in position of the multiple bond and the asterisk from one end of the three-atom grouping to the other: X=Y–Z* becomes *X–Y=Z.

prompt: Which atoms can be X, Y, and Z in the general three-atom resonance grouping?

choices.text: C, N, O, P, S, or others
Only carbon
choices.why: Oxygen often appears, as in acetate and carbonate, and N, P and S can too.

choices.text: Only second-row atoms such as C, N and O
choices.why: Third-row atoms such as P and S can be part of the grouping too, as in the methyl phosphate anion.

choices.text: Only atoms that carry a formal charge
choices.why: The requirement is a p orbital on each atom, not a charge on each atom.

explanation: The atoms X, Y, and Z in the general structure might be C, N, O, P, S, or others, as long as each has a p orbital.

prompt: What is the strategy for drawing resonance forms of a larger structure?

choices.text: Find a multiple bond next to an atom with a p orbital, then exchange the multiple bond and the electrons in that p orbital
Move hydrogen atoms to other positions and redraw the bonds
choices.why: Moving atoms gives a different compound, not a resonance form.

choices.text: Break each single bond in turn and form a new one elsewhere
choices.why: σ bonds and connections stay the same; only π and nonbonding electrons move.

choices.text: Add a lone pair to each atom until all are charged
choices.why: Every resonance form has the same electrons; they are only rearranged.

explanation: Look for three-atom groupings that contain a multiple bond next to an atom with a p orbital. Then exchange the positions of the multiple bond and the electrons in the p orbital. Repeating this for each grouping generates all the resonance forms.

prompt: Removing H^+ from 2,4-pentanedione with a base gives an anion. How many resonance structures does this anion have?
explanation: The anion has a lone pair and negative charge on the central carbon, with a C=O bond on each side. Each O=C–C:− grouping gives one more resonance form, so there are three: the charge on the central carbon or on either oxygen.

prompt: In the anion formed when a base removes H^+ from 2,4-pentanedione, where are the lone pair and formal negative charge when the anion is first drawn?

choices.text: On the central carbon, between two C=O bonds
On one of the oxygen atoms only
choices.why: Charge on oxygen appears in other resonance forms; as first drawn, the base leaves the lone pair on the central carbon.

choices.text: On a carbon at the end of the chain
choices.why: The H^+ is removed from the central carbon, which lies between the two C=O groups.

choices.text: On a carbonyl carbon
choices.why: The charge is on the carbon next to the carbonyl carbons, so that each O=C–C:− grouping can show resonance.

explanation: The 2,4-pentanedione anion has a lone pair of electrons and a formal negative charge on the central carbon atom, next to a C=O bond on the left and another on the right.

prompt: Why does the 2,4-pentanedione anion have three resonance structures rather than two?

choices.text: There is a C=O bond on each side of the carbon with the lone pair, giving two O=C–C:− groupings
The molecule has five carbon atoms
choices.why: The number of carbons doesn't set the count; the number of three-atom groupings around the lone pair does.

choices.text: The negative charge can also move onto a CH3 carbon
choices.why: The CH3 carbons aren't part of an O=C–C:− grouping with the lone pair; only the central carbon and the two oxygens carry the charge.

choices.text: Each oxygen has three lone pairs
choices.why: The count comes from the two C=O bonds next to the carbanion, each forming a three-atom grouping with it.

explanation: The O=C–C:− grouping on the left gives two resonance structures. Just as there is a C=O bond to the left of the lone pair, there is a second C=O bond to the right, so a total of three resonance structures can be drawn.

prompt: How many resonance structures can be drawn for the carbonate ion, CO3^2−?
explanation: Each singly bonded, negatively charged oxygen sits next to the C=O double bond. Exchanging the double bond and a lone pair in each grouping puts the double bond on each of the three oxygens in turn, giving three resonance structures.

prompt: In any one resonance structure of the carbonate ion, CO3^2−, how many oxygen atoms carry a negative charge?
explanation: Each resonance structure has one C=O double bond and two singly bonded oxygens, each with three lone pairs and a negative charge, for the ion's total charge of 2−.

prompt: In a resonance structure of the carbonate ion, how many lone pairs are on a singly bonded, negatively charged oxygen atom?
explanation: In carbonate, each singly bonded oxygen atom has three lone pairs and a negative charge, and is adjacent to the C=O double bond, whose oxygen has two lone pairs.

choices.text: A substance with a single, unpaired electron in one of its orbitals
An ion with a negative charge
choices.why: An anion has extra electrons, usually paired; a radical is defined by one unpaired electron.

choices.text: A substance with an empty p orbital
choices.why: A vacant p orbital is found in a cation such as the allyl cation; a radical's orbital holds one electron.

choices.text: Any substance that has resonance forms
choices.why: Many substances with resonance forms, such as acetate, are not radicals.

explanation: A radical is a substance that contains a single, unpaired electron in one of its orbitals, denoted by a dot (·).

prompt: How many resonance forms does the pentadienyl radical have?
explanation: The unpaired electron on an end carbon sits next to a C=C bond, giving a second form with the electron on the central carbon. There it is next to the other C=C bond, giving a third form with the electron on the other end carbon.

prompt: In the resonance forms of the pentadienyl radical, on which carbons does the unpaired electron appear?

choices.text: The two end carbons and the central carbon
All five carbons
choices.why: Each shift moves the electron two atoms along a three-atom grouping, so it skips the second and fourth carbons.

choices.text: Only the two end carbons
choices.why: Moving the electron from an end carbon across one C=C bond puts it on the central carbon first.

choices.text: Only the second and fourth carbons
choices.why: Those carbons are the middle atoms of the three-atom groupings, so the electron never lands on them.

explanation: In the three resonance forms of the pentadienyl radical, the unpaired electron is on the right-most carbon, the central carbon, and the left-most carbon. Each exchange moves it from one end of a three-atom grouping to the other.

prompt: In the allyl cation, H2C=CH–CH2^+, what does the p orbital on the CH2^+ carbon contain?

choices.text: Nothing: it is vacant
A lone pair of electrons
choices.why: A lone pair on carbon gives a negative charge, as in the 2,4-pentanedione anion. A positive carbon has an empty p orbital.

choices.text: A single unpaired electron
choices.why: That describes a radical carbon, such as in the pentadienyl radical, which is neutral.

choices.text: Two π electrons from the C=C bond
choices.why: Those electrons belong to the double bond in this form; in the other resonance form they shift to the C–CH2 bond.

explanation: The allyl cation is a three-atom grouping X=Y–Z* in which the asterisk is a vacant p orbital. Exchanging the double bond and the vacant orbital gives its two resonance forms, with the positive charge on either end carbon.
